title: Lesson Observations: Supportive Leadership or Surveillance Culture?
author: Samuel Kammin
summary: Samuel Kammin uses a school visit to St John the Baptist in Woking to ask when classroom observation supports teachers and when it becomes surveillance. He traces the growth of surveillance in education to national crises and accountability regimes, including England's 2013 removal of the three-hour limit on lesson observations. At St John, senior leaders conduct daily learning walks through every classroom to foster a supportive team environment and flatten the hierarchy. Kammin weighs the benefits (seeing practice first hand, sharing good ideas, reducing isolation) against the limits of a brief snapshot, and uses Foucault's panopticon and the synopticon to frame the risk of teachers performing for observers. A Finnish comparator, where co-teaching replaces leader observation, suggests collegial collaboration can deliver some of the same benefits. He concludes that visibility is acceptable only if it leads to honest professional dialogue and preserves trust.
points: Daily learning walks can be supportive, but their value depends on whether leaders treat what they see as a starting point for inquiry rather than a verdict.
A few minutes in a classroom cannot establish what pupils have learned over time or why a teacher made a decision.
The panopticon and synopticon framework shows how observation can push teachers to perform for whoever might be watching, while schools themselves feel watched by inspectors.
Finnish co-teaching suggests collegial observation can replace some leader surveillance, though Kammin warns against assuming it transfers directly.
The key test is whether observation makes professional openness easier or harder to sustain.
quotes: The question I have been interested in this week is specifically in relation to lesson observations, namely, when do classroom observations support teachers, and when do they become surveillance?
The purpose, as the deputy head explained, is to foster a supportive team environment and establish a leadership presence across the school.
Unfortunately, a brief visit will rarely tell the whole story, but a snapshot is not nothing, especially not snapshots that are taken every single day in every classroom.
As I mentioned, a few minutes in a classroom can offer a snapshot of teaching, but it cannot reliably establish what children have learned over time or why a teacher has made particular decisions.
The crucial distinction is whether observation encourages honest professional dialogue or leaves teachers feeling that they must continually demonstrate competence.

Perhaps school surveillance is better thought of as a searchlight rather than a panopticon; in many cases, teachers are aware that they are being observed, unlike the panopticon prisoners that can only guess.

Accountability matters, but so does the trust that allows teachers to acknowledge difficulties, experiment and improve. The question for school leaders is whether their presence makes that professional openness easier or harder to sustain.
